newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma City bomb suspects to get separate trials.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma City bomb suspects to get separate trials.

text.p: A judge handed the two defendants in the Oklahoma City bombing trial a major victory on Friday by ordering separate trials for them, saying there was no other way to give them a fair hearing.
U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch also ordered that Timothy McVeigh be tried before co-defendant Terry Nichols.
"A joint trial of these defendants presents such an unacceptable risk of prejudice to both of them as to require separate trials," Matsch said in a 20-page decision.
McVeigh and Nichols, former U.S. Army buddies, are accused of the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City, which killed 168 people.
Both defendants urged the judge to grant separate trials because, they said, their defences might have to be based in part on pointing the finger of blame at each other.
Their attorneys had argued at a pre-trial hearing that in a sense, each defence lawyer would become a second prosecutor in the courtroom and this would be unfair to the defendants.

Nichols' attorney, Michael Tigar, said now each defendant would be viewed individually. "A separate trial will force the government to prove its case against Mr. Nichols, rather than merely rely on guilt by association and spillover prejudice from the case against Mr. McVeigh," Tigar said.

Matsch also said the conflict between the two defendants is "even more apparent" when viewed in the context of sentencing, because "each defendant will try to portray the other as a more culpable perpetrator of the crime." The two could be sentenced to death if convicted.

McVeigh's attorney, Stephen Jones, said the decision "clears the underbrush," allowing him to focus on the facts to be presented at the trial, a date for which has not been set. Jones said the decision represented McVeigh's fourth major objective.

The other three were the removal of a federal judge in Oklahoma, the transfer of the trial to Denver and the decision that statements Nichols made to authorities two days after the bombing could not be used against McVeigh.
The trial was moved to Denver in order to ensure a fairer hearing.

Key in the judge's decision were statements Nichols made in Herington, Kansas, during a nine-hour session with authorities just days after the bombing. They remain under seal and can only be used against Nichols and not McVeigh, Matsch previously ruled. Nichols mentioned McVeigh's name more than 60 times, McVeigh's lawyers have said.

Nichols is not expected to take the stand, meaning McVeigh's lawyers could not cross-examine him, depriving McVeigh of his right under the Sixth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution to confront witnesses against him.
McVeigh's defence team did not want the Nichols statement to be used, for instance, because Nichols said both he and McVeigh were in Oklahoma City just days before the bombing.
Because the two will be tried separately, the Nichols statement will not even come up in McVeigh's trial.
